summary.text: Composites are excluded by counting the factors divisible by each odd prime power via the multiplicative order of \(2\), then comparing the resulting valuations with Legendre’s formula to force an odd prime divisor of \(n\) to divide \(a(n-1)\); powers of two are handled by an exact \(2\)-adic valuation using \(s_2(2^k-1)=k\). For prime \(n\), Wilson’s theorem and the product identity turn the assumed congruence into \(\prod_{1\le k<n-1}(2^k-1)\equiv1\pmod n\), so any order of \(2\) smaller than \(n-1\) would make one factor zero, forcing the order to be \(n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_M:=\prod_{j=1}^{M-1}(2^j-1)\qquad(M\geq 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
a(M)=\frac{2^{M-1}P_M}{M!}.
\]
We will first establish that this quotient is an integer, together with a more precise divisibility statement that will be used to exclude composite values of \(n\).

Throughout, for a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\).

## 1. Counting prime powers in the factors \(2^j-1\)

We need two elementary counting facts.

First, if \(P\geq 2\) and \(m\geq 0\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac mP\right\rfloor
 \leq
\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{P-1}\right\rfloor,
\tag{1}
\]
where, when \(m=0\), the right side may simply be interpreted as \(0\). Indeed, put \(q=\lfloor m/P\rfloor\). If \(q=0\), the assertion is immediate. If \(q>0\), then \(qP\leq m\), and hence
\[
q(P-1)=qP-q\leq m-1.
\]
This proves (1).

Now let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(i\geq 1\). Since \(2\) is relatively prime to \(p^i\), it has a multiplicative order modulo \(p^i\); denote it by
\[
d_i=\operatorname{ord}_{p^i}(2).
\]
Euler's theorem gives
\[
d_i\mid \varphi(p^i).
\]
In particular \(d_i>0\), and because \(p^i\geq 2\) and \(\varphi(p^i)<p^i\),
\[
d_i\leq p^i-1.
\tag{2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
p^i\mid 2^j-1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_i\mid j.
\tag{3}
\]
Consequently, among \(j=1,\ldots,B\), the number for which \(p^i\mid 2^j-1\) is exactly
\[
\left\lfloor\frac B{d_i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{4}
\]
Combining (1), (2), and (4), we obtain
\[
\#\{1\leq j\leq B:p^i\mid 2^j-1\}
 =\left\lfloor\frac B{d_i}\right\rfloor
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac B{p^i-1}\right\rfloor
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac{B+1}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{5}
\]

We will also require a strict version when \(i=1\). Suppose \(n=pt\), where \(p\) is odd prime and \(t\geq 2\). Then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{pt-1}{p}\right\rfloor=t-1.
\tag{6}
\]
On the other hand, the number of \(j\) in the range \(1\leq j\leq pt-2\) satisfying \(p\mid 2^j-1\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{pt-2}{d_1}\right\rfloor
\geq \left\lfloor\frac{pt-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since
\[
t(p-1)=pt-t\leq pt-2
\]
for \(t\geq2\), this last quantity is at least \(t\). Thus
\[
\#\{1\leq j\leq pt-2:p\mid 2^j-1\}
\geq \left\lfloor\frac{pt-1}{p}\right\rfloor+1.
\tag{7}
\]

## 2. Valuations of the product and integrality of \(a(M)\)

For any finite collection of positive integers \(x_j\), one has
\[
v_p\left(\prod_jx_j\right)=\sum_jv_p(x_j).
\]
Also,
\[
v_p(x)=\sum_{i\geq1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid x}.
\]
Interchanging these two finite sums gives the useful identity
\[
v_p(P_M)
 =\sum_{i\geq1}\#\{1\leq j\leq M-1:p^i\mid 2^j-1\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Only finitely many summands are nonzero. For example, if \(1\leq j<M\), then
\[
2^j-1<2^M\leq p^M,
\]
so no exponent \(i\geq M\) is needed when \(p\geq2\).

Legendre's formula says
\[
v_p(M!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac M{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{9}
\]
For odd \(p\), apply (5) with \(B=M-1\) to every summand in (8). This yields
\[
v_p(P_M)\geq
\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac M{p^i}\right\rfloor
=v_p(M!).
\tag{10}
\]
For \(p=2\), the elementary estimate
\[
v_2(M!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac M{2^i}\right\rfloor<M
\]
shows, since the valuation is integral, that
\[
v_2(M!)\leq M-1=v_2(2^{M-1}).
\tag{11}
\]
Equations (10) and (11) show, prime by prime, that
\[
M!\mid 2^{M-1}P_M.
\tag{12}
\]
Thus \(a(M)\) is indeed an integer, and its defining quotient satisfies the exact identity
\[
a(M)M!=2^{M-1}P_M.
\tag{13}
\]

We now sharpen (10) in the situation needed for a composite number. Let \(n=pt\), with \(p\) an odd prime and \(t\geq2\), and put \(M=n-1\). Applying (5) to all powers \(p^i\), and applying the strict estimate (7) for \(i=1\), equations (8) and (9) give
\[
v_p(P_{n-1})\geq v_p((n-1)!)+1.
\tag{14}
\]
Indeed, the \(i\)-th summand on the factorial side is
\(\lfloor(n-1)/p^i\rfloor\), while the corresponding product summand counts \(j\) with \(1\leq j\leq n-2\) and \(p^i\mid2^j-1\). Estimate (5) gives a weak inequality for every \(i\), and (7) supplies one additional unit at \(i=1\).

Since \(p\) is odd, \(v_p(2^{n-2})=0\). Taking \(p\)-adic valuations in (13), with \(M=n-1\), therefore gives
\[
v_p(a(n-1))+v_p((n-1)!)=v_p(P_{n-1}).
\]
By (14),
\[
v_p(a(n-1))\geq1,
\]
so we have proved:

**Odd-factor lemma.** If \(p\) is an odd prime, \(p\mid n\), and \(n\geq2p\), then
\[
p\mid a(n-1).
\tag{15}
\]

## 3. Excluding composites with an odd prime factor

Suppose \(p\) is an odd prime divisor of \(n\), with \(n\geq2p\). If
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2},
\tag{16}
\]
then, since \(p\mid n\), we also have
\[
p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
But (15) says \(p\mid a(n-1)\). Subtracting gives
\[
p\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must divide \(2\), so this forces \(p=2\), contrary to the fact that \(p\) is odd. Hence (16) is impossible whenever such an odd prime factor exists.

## 4. Excluding powers of two

It remains to handle composite numbers with no odd prime factor. Let
\[
n=2^k,\qquad k\geq2,
\]
and put
\[
m=n-1=2^k-1.
\]
Every factor \(2^j-1\) is odd, so
\[
v_2(P_m)=0.
\tag{17}
\]
We also need the exact valuation of \(m!\). A standard consequence of Legendre's formula is
\[
v_2(r!)=r-s_2(r),
\tag{18}
\]
where \(s_2(r)\) denotes the sum of the binary digits of \(r\). For completeness, if
\(r=\sum_{ell\geq0}\varepsilon_ell2^ell\), with each \(\varepsilon_ell\in\{0,1\}\), then
\[
\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac r{2^i}\right\rfloor
=\sum_{ell\geq0}\varepsilon_ell(2^ell-1)
=r-\sum_{ell\geq0}\varepsilon_ell,
\]
which proves (18). The binary expansion of \(2^k-1\) consists of exactly \(k\) ones. Hence
\[
v_2(m!)=m-k.
\tag{19}
\]
Taking \(2\)-adic valuations in (13), and using (17), gives
\[
v_2(a(m))+v_2(m!)=m-1.
\]
Together with (19), this yields
\[
v_2(a(2^k-1))=k-1.
\tag{20}
\]
In particular,
\[
2^k\nmid a(2^k-1).
\tag{21}
\]

On the other hand, for every \(k\geq2\),
\[
k\leq2^k-2.
\tag{22}
\]
This follows immediately by induction (there is equality at \(k=2\), and doubling \(2^k\) increases faster than increasing \(k\) by one). Therefore
\[
2^k\mid 2^{2^k-2}.
\tag{23}
\]
If \(2^k\) divided
\[
a(2^k-1)+2^{2^k-2},
\]
then subtracting the second summand, which is divisible by \(2^k\) by (23), would imply \(2^k\mid a(2^k-1)\), contradicting (21). Thus no power \(2^k\) with \(k\geq2\) satisfies the assumed divisibility.

## 5. Every composite \(n>2\) is excluded

Let \(n>2\) be composite. Write
\[
n=2^k m
\]
with \(m\) odd. If \(m=1\), then \(n=2^k\); because \(n>2\), we have \(k\geq2\), and the preceding section excludes \(n\).

Suppose instead that \(m>1\), and let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(m\), for instance its least prime divisor. Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\) is odd, and of course \(p\mid n\). Write \(n=pc\). If \(c=1\), then \(n=p\) would be prime, contrary to assumption. Hence \(c\geq2\), so \(n\geq2p\). Section 3 now excludes \(n\).

We have therefore proved that if \(n>2\) and
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2},
\tag{24}
\]
then \(n\) must be prime.

## 6. For prime \(n\), the order of \(2\) is \(n-1\)

Assume henceforth that \(n>2\) is prime and that (24) holds. Work modulo \(n\). Identity (13), with \(M=n-1\), says
\[
a(n-1)(n-1)!
 =2^{n-2}\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1).
\tag{25}
\]
By Wilson's theorem,
\[
(n-1)!\equiv-1\pmod n.
\tag{26}
\]
The assumed divisibility (24) is equivalent to
\[
a(n-1)\equiv-2^{n-2}\pmod n.
\tag{27}
\]
Substituting (26) and (27) into (25), its left side becomes
\[
(-2^{n-2})(-1)=2^{n-2}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{n-2}\equiv
2^{n-2}\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1)
pmod n.
\]
Because \(n>2\) is prime, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\), and hence \(2^{n-2}\) is invertible modulo \(n\). Cancelling it gives the crucial identity
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1)\equiv1\pmod n.
\tag{28}
\]

Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\). Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
d\mid n-1.
\tag{29}
\]
In particular, \(1\leq d\leq n-1\). If \(d<n-1\), then \(d\) lies in the range \(1\leq d\leq n-2\), and the factor of the product (28) corresponding to \(j=d\) is
\[
2^d-1\equiv0\pmod n.
\]
The whole product on the left of (28) would then be congruent to \(0\), contradicting its congruence to \(1\). Therefore \(d\) cannot be less than \(n-1\). Together with (29), this proves
\[
\operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1.
\tag{30}
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Equation (30) says exactly that \(2\) has order \(\varphi(n)\) modulo \(n\), i.e. that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Combining Sections 5 and 6, for every integer \(n>2\), the divisibility
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
implies that \(n\) is prime and that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
